fields.Front: What really distinguishes association, aggregation, and composition?
fields.Back: Ownership and lifetime. Association: two objects exist independently and merely know about each other (teacher/student). Composition: the part belongs to the whole and dies with it (engine/car), filled diamond. Aggregation sits between: the whole holds parts that can outlive it, hollow diamond.

fields.Front: How do composition and aggregation map onto C++ member declarations?
fields.Back: Composition is a member held by value (Paypal processor;), created and destroyed with the owner. Aggregation is a member held by reference or pointer (IPaymentProcessor& processor;), bound in the constructor to an object that lives elsewhere.

fields.Front: In the e-commerce class diagram, which classes inherit from User, and what does User contain?
fields.Back: Customer and Administrator inherit from User, with hollow-headed arrows pointing up at it. User has -userId: string, -password: string, -loginStatus: string, -registerDate: date, and +verifyLogin(): bool.

fields.Front: In the e-commerce class diagram, what does Customer own and with what multiplicities?
fields.Back: Two filled-diamond compositions: to Shopping Cart with 1 at Customer and 0..* at Shopping Cart, and to Orders with 1 at Customer and 0..* at Orders. Customer's own attributes include -customerName, -address, -email, -creditCardInfo, -shippingInfo, -accountBalance: float.

fields.Front: In the e-commerce class diagram, what does Orders own?
fields.Back: Shipping Info (composition, 1 to 1) and Order Details (composition, 1 to 1, with the line labelled 'has a'). Orders itself has -orderId, -dateCreated, -dateShipped, -customerName, -customerId, -status, -shippingId, and +placeOrder().

fields.Front: What encapsulation discipline is visible in the e-commerce class diagram?
fields.Back: Every attribute is marked - (private) and every method is marked + (public): data hidden, behaviour exposed. Also, inheritance arrows point UP to User and the diamonds sit at the OWNER (Customer owns carts and orders; Orders owns its details and shipping info).

fields.Front: Multiplicity: what does a plain line with no numbers between A and B mean?
fields.Back: One B with each A; one A with each B. Drawing 1 at each end with arrowheads both ways means the same thing, made explicit and navigable in both directions.

fields.Front: Multiplicity: what does 1 at A and * at B mean, and what does * at both ends mean?
fields.Back: 1-*: zero or more Bs with each A, and one A with each B. *-*: zero or more Bs with each A and zero or more As with each B, i.e. many-to-many.

fields.Front: Multiplicity: what does 1 at A and 2..5 at B mean, and how do you read multiplicities generally?
fields.Back: Two to five Bs with each A; one A with each B. Rule: the number written at the B end says how many Bs relate to ONE A, and vice versa. * alone is zero or more, 1..* is one or more, 0..1 is optional, 2..5 is a bounded range.

fields.Front: What does a single arrowhead from A to B with * at B mean?
fields.Back: Zero or more Bs with each A, and B knows nothing about A: the association is navigable only from A to B. That is how you would draw Checkout -> IPaymentProcessor, since Checkout knows its processor but the processor knows nothing about Checkout.

fields.Front: What three pieces of guidance are given for refining a class diagram?
fields.Back: Design is iterative, so expect to redraw as understanding improves; avoid overcomplicating diagrams; each class should represent a clear, distinct concept, which is another way of saying high cohesion.

fields.Text: A UML class box has three compartments, top to bottom: {{c1::name}}, {{c1::attributes}}, {{c1::methods}}.
UML visibility markers: {{c1::-}} means private, {{c1::+}} means public, {{c1::#}} means protected.
fields.Extra: Written before the member name, followed by a colon and the type: -balance: float, +deposit(): void.

fields.Text: Class diagram lines: a {{c1::solid line}} for association, an {{c1::arrow (hollow triangular head)}} for inheritance pointing at the base class, and a {{c1::diamond}} for composition, placed at the side of the whole.
fields.Extra: A filled diamond denotes composition; a hollow diamond denotes aggregation.

fields.Text: Class relationships as phrases: association is {{c1::has-a}} (a teacher has a student), inheritance is {{c1::is-a}} (Admin is a type of User), composition is {{c1::strong has-a}} (a Car contains an Engine).

In the e-commerce diagram, Customer owns Shopping Cart and Orders with multiplicity {{c1::1}} at Customer and {{c1::0..*}} at each, while Orders owns Shipping Info and Order Details at {{c1::1 to 1}}.
Multiplicity shorthand: * means {{c1::zero or more}}, 1..* means {{c1::one or more}}, 0..1 means {{c1::optional}}, 2..5 means {{c1::two to five}}.
fields.Extra: The number at the B end says how many Bs go with one A.
